Vira Toland recalls the 1919 milk-testing scandal at Ostrey Hollow station, where accusations of water in the cans led to the discovery that station operator Ansel Keddie was skimming cream, destroying his reputation and severing families for decades.
The document is from 1966 and does not contain information about 1908; it recommends six mills on the dollar for 1967.

Effie Loomis, former secretary of the Creamery Association, documents the organization's founding and Article VII on butter fat testing, culminating in the 1925 arbitration that awarded Ostrey Hollow patrons $3,800 without establishing cause while omitting what the official record excluded.
The play being performed at the Ellerby Playhouse is *The Sparrow Hotel*.

Ansel Keddie, the station tester, describes his rigorous testing methods, the persistent anomaly of 1911 when a borrowed measure was used, and how he was dismissed despite the board finding "no cause established," unable to explain why Ostrey Hollow's milk consistently tested lower than other herds.
The wholesale order Elias Norcross placed with Purcell & Weare on 14 March 1932 was $59.65.

Ivy Keddie, Ansel's granddaughter, reveals that the station's condemned pipettes were defective, delivering only 95% of the correct charge, making all tests 5% low and accounting for the full 19-hundredth gap—vindicating her grandfather decades after his dismissal and death.
Tamsin Ochoa's service number is 4471-K.

Wilbur Teague, the Association's bookkeeper, explains the "station gain" line he invented—a consistent 5.25% discrepancy between credited and received butterfat—and notes that he warned manager Vose in 1916 but was told to let it alone, defending his role as bookkeeper rather than conscience.
Judge Thurlow Vane's court imposed a fine of $5.00 on Delia Fought for the petty theft of dress goods.

Merle Strawn, state dairy inspector, documents his 28 years on circuit with clinical field notes, including the crucial June 1923 entry condemning Ostrey Hollow's pipettes as delivering short of their mark and ordering replacements verified in October 1923.
Lemma 2.1 is given the name "Interleaving."

Halbert Nym, a museum curator, catalogs 16 archival items documenting the Ostrey Hollow scandal from its origins through the 1925 arbitration award and the 1958 scientific proof that defective pipettes delivered only 95% of their marked capacity, exonerating the station and its tester.
Mr. Ansgar Krell remained at the Cold Spring Water-Cure for 4 weeks, from 3 May to 31 May 1884.

Selby Vose, the manager, defends the $3,800 settlement and attributes Ostrey Hollow's low tests to deliberate water-adulteration by patrons rather than equipment failure, pointing to the sudden 21-hundredth test improvement in 1924 when the Association began scrutinizing the station.
The error code `SKF-2201` is returned when a sailings query span exceeds 14 days.

Roy Brant (farmer): his father's ledger shows perfect agreement between farm and station scales across thirty years despite persistent 17/100ths shortfall below Larrow Green, and documents family kinship to Ansel Keddie.
Dr. Pemberton charged $8.00 for the confinement and mileage of Mrs. Content Averill on January 3, 1906.

Rosalie Cudd (cheesemaker at Alder Corners): the four Hessel Bottom farmers' milk tested consistently 3.78–3.82 across sixteen summers at her factory, proving it was good milk, and watered milk would have been immediately evident in cheese production.
The man's crown will cost him $1,480 after insurance.

Leland Vaught (professor of dairy husbandry): Bulletin 471 definitively proves the 26-year shortfall at Ostrey Hollow was caused by pipettes delivering 16.27 c.c. instead of marked 17.6 c.c., vindicated by the 1911 interval when borrowed measure raised tests to 3.80.
The color named in the third paragraph is vermilion, describing Bettine Rausch's apron.

Dell Rundle (schoolteacher): fifty-year jubilee recounting the Association from 1889, Article VII's payment rule, the Ostrey Hollow complaint and 1925 arbitration, and her retraction upon discovering ledgers show cream arrived heavier than credited, ruling out theft.
Message No. 219, filed by Perley Dunmore, reading "FATHER VERY LOW COME AT ONCE," contained 6 words.

Alonzo Frick (attorney): arbitration chairman's recollection of the 1925 board hearing three contradictory explanations (water, cream theft, hay), Keddie's honest denial, the Association's dismissal of him mid-proceedings, and the board's uncomfortable award without finding cause.
The locksmith's dog is named Buckley, a bad-tempered gray terrier.

Hobart Sill (buttermaker of 41 years): the Hollow's cream consistently arrived heavier than credited, he suspects water was deliberately added (evidenced by sudden improvement in the 1920s), but defends the cows while condemning the men.
The norm defined in Definition 1.3 is called the Trebbin norm.

Nyle Grigg (committee chairman): reprints his 1908 report blaming wet hay for low Hollow tests, citing State Agricultural College Bulletin 214 as vindication that bog hay depresses butterfat by two tenths.

Dr. Roland Kepp (veterinary surgeon): scientific evidence that wet bog meadows naturally depress butterfat—two tenths per College Bulletin 214, matching Ostrey Hollow's 21/100ths complaint—through mineral-poor herbage and cow physiology, not equipment or fraud.
Phyl warns Armando not to use dryer eleven, which takes money and turns for only forty seconds before quitting.

Hazel Brant recounts her grandfather's weigh book documenting the consistent 19/100ths shortfall, reveals Ansel Keddie's kinship to the Brants, the condemned glassware sitting unaddressed in the loft, and how her cousin Ivy discovered the faulty pipettes had caused the discrepancy all along.
The color named in the third paragraph is magenta, describing the scarf worn by the woman called Tuesday.

Duncan Keddie documents his father Ansel's family kinship to the Brants, recalls that Ansel suspected faulty glass in 1911 but recorded only a question mark, and traces how all the key documents (test books, notebooks, and the condemned crate) were dispersed to historical repositories where his daughter Ivy discovered the evidence.
The coroner's jury found that Obadiah Chalmers came to his death by drowning in the mill pond resulting from an accidental fall from the flume edge while at his work, without evidence of foul play.

The Ashlin Chronicle reports that Ivy Keddie's 1958 college bulletin clears the long-dead Ansel Keddie by proving the condemned pipettes in the station loft averaged 16.27 c.c. instead of marked 17.6 c.c., costing patrons $19,600 and implicating the 1897 supplier of deliberately short glass.
The total ice-out pot in the spring of 1996 was six thousand eight hundred and forty dollars.

Junia Ammon documents Ammon & Sons' glassware trade, reproduces the April 1897 invoice for the Ostrey Hollow pipettes, recalls their vague 1923 reply that works records had burned, and reflects that the short delivery was likely an undetected mold error the company should have acknowledged to a quarter-century customer.
In Proposition 4.1, the cycle used in the sharpness example is a 7-cycle.

Cleve Oram recounts 70 years on the cream wagon, recalls the 1925 hearing held at the station with the faulty glassware crate directly overhead in the loft, records his father's lifelong belief that cream was vanishing before reaching the platform, and describes Ansel Keddie's quiet competence and dismissal.

Orin Falke provides an official 1959 county report demolishing water/theft/hay explanations, detailing the 1911 glass replacement experiment and 1923 condemnation, concluding that Ivy Keddie's 1958 discovery of faulty pipettes proves the 19/100ths shortfall, and withdrawing earlier concessions about wet hay after reviewing Bulletin 214.
Russ's wife's name is Dorrit.

Bertram Kyle describes 25 years ruling the office ledgers, records the annual 5.25% station "gain as usual" as an unexplained figure, notes the 1919 water-warning letter and 1922 condemned glass incident, and reflects that the real failure was having everything visible with a name on it, which made it invisible.
The color named in the third paragraph is teal, describing the endpapers of the collected edition containing Halvane's famous diagram.

Orra Keddie's diary records the station's May 1897 glass arrival, the 1908 hay-blame committee, Ansel's distress over poor testing, the June 1919 water-warning letters he personally delivered, the July 1923 new glass, and his April 1925 dismissal after 29 seasons, followed by his 1934 death unnamed and uncleared until 24 years after.
The total toll collected at the Wren's Bend bridge for the week of June 5–11, 1899 was $13.88.
